title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Q&A Session with Mis Propias Finanzas on September 20, 2022
summary: A Q&A with a Colombian personal-finance channel covering the $650,000 Buffett lunch and the friendships with Munger and Rick Guerin it produced, Pabrai's step-by-step process for researching a company (VIC write-ups, decades of shareholder letters, transcripts, proxies), his views on inheritance and the UGMA accounts for his daughters, Dakshana's measurable-outcomes approach, Munger's mental-model hacks for choosing people, and how to filter Turkish stocks by hard-currency revenue.

ideas.idea: The $650,000 Buffett lunch in 2007 was a tuition bill for the $84 million he had made from Buffett, Munger and Graham, and it turned out to be 'buy one, get infinite free'.
ideas.detail: He was prepared to bid $2 million; Guy Spier was capped at $250,000 for a third. The lunch led to years of lunches and Friday bridge with Munger at the LA Country Club and annual invitations to Buffett's Sunday brunch in Omaha from 2007 to 2022.

ideas.idea: Buffett turned an innocent question about Rick Guerin into a lesson on leverage: Rick was levered in 1973-74 and had to sell Berkshire to Buffett at $40 a share, now over $400,000.
ideas.detail: That is 10,000x in under 50 years. Buffett's mindset at the lunch is that whoever paid should feel they got a bargain, so he works hard to deliver value.

ideas.idea: If you are wondering whether something is in your circle of competence, the answer is that it is not.
ideas.detail: Inside the circle you would know how to value the business, how it makes money and its likely trajectory within ranges. The same hack applies to crypto: outside the circle, no opinion needed.

ideas.idea: His research process starts by looking for a reason to stop: first who the admired shareholders are, then all Value Investors Club write-ups and comments, then 20-30 years of shareholder letters, then transcript Q&A, then proxies, and only then the financials.
ideas.detail: Reading old letters with hindsight (2005-07 before the 2008 tsunami, 2018-19 before the pandemic) shows how resilient the model is and whether management underpromises and overdelivers. Transcript Q&A is valuable because it is not written by a PR firm; proxies reveal dilution and comp plans.

ideas.idea: Talking to management is irrelevant to the thesis for large US companies, but for non-US companies he would not invest without plenty of interaction with the CEO and senior management.
ideas.detail: He has met Micron's CEO Sanjay Mehrotra and its CFO but says none of it mattered to the thesis; large US companies rarely let you past IR.

ideas.idea: He has a 10% limit on what he will invest in a single business, but Micron grew to 20-25% of the portfolio through appreciation.
ideas.detail: After the 2022 price drop it may be somewhat less; he declines to discuss current holdings until they are sold.

ideas.idea: Large inheritances do more harm than good; his father's bankruptcy when he was 20 was one of the best things that happened to him because it made clear no inheritance was coming.
ideas.detail: Buffett's Jesse Owens analogy: start the son at the 10-meter line, not the 40-meter line. A large inheritance is an IV drip, the same as welfare for 'trust fund babies'.

ideas.idea: He funded UGMA accounts of $10,000 a year for each daughter, managed them with three or four stocks, and gave full control at 18 on the theory that 18 years is enough to transfer values.
ideas.detail: The accounts compounded to seven figures; he told his daughters at 12-13 that nothing else was coming and to pursue passion rather than pay. Inheritances should arrive before 30-35 when trajectory changes are still possible. Daughter Monsoon used the money as confidence to quit her job and launch a fund.

ideas.idea: Charities need to be good at capital allocation, so Dakshana only pursues endeavors where outcomes can be measured easily, which biased it toward education.
ideas.detail: In 2006-07 he found most charities had good hearts but no business sense, and 97-98% of causes (e.g. needle distribution for the homeless) cannot be measured. Following Munger's 'always invert', he limited himself to measurable outcomes.

ideas.idea: Dakshana takes over the education of very poor 16-18 year olds and gets 70-80% into the IITs or top medical schools, versus a 1-2% base rate.
ideas.detail: Over 1.4 million apply for 15,000 IIT seats and 2 million for 10-15,000 medical seats; once in, the schools are nearly free. After 15 years the oldest alumni are approaching 30 with flourishing careers.

ideas.idea: His job description is reading, thinking and talking; as an introvert he finds drilling into a company's VIC reports and letters an 'orgasmic experience'.
ideas.detail: His favorite genre is biographies and autobiographies of business leaders, because they show what drove them and the long history of the business.

ideas.idea: The one book to read is Poor Charlie's Almanack, especially 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment', which took Munger 50 years of wisdom to write and gives a huge advantage in life.
ideas.detail: He rereads it every year and finds new things. Munger's edge is horsepower plus 400-500 books a year for 80 years (about 40,000 books) plus the third hack of mental models.

ideas.idea: Buffett and Munger's people hack: bring only the obvious top 3-4% into your circle and treat the unknown 92% the same as the bad ones, because 3% of infinity is still infinity.
ideas.detail: Buffett told him he is not a great judge of humans; at a party of 100 he could identify 3-4 great and 3-4 bad and could not rank the rest. Excluding a great person carries no penalty, like passing on a great company, but including a bad one does. Pabrai's own hack: every friend of Charlie is a friend of mine.

ideas.idea: Knowing your exit date is a huge advantage because you can plan backwards; life is all about how many doubles you get.
ideas.detail: Life expectancy calculators moved his expected death from June 11, 2044 to 2054-2056; the extra 10-12 years mean two to four more doubles. Buffett's genie wish: 'when they look at my corpse, they say, man, he was old', purely to maximize the compounding runway.

ideas.idea: Beginners must make real investments with real money rather than paper portfolios, expect a 33-50% error rate even if very good, and learn from their own and others' mistakes.
ideas.detail: Cites John Templeton's one-third to one-half error rate for really good investors; trading costs are low so even $5,000-10,000 is enough to start after doing the work.

ideas.idea: Turkey is the most interesting geography because it is the most dislocated market with the most extreme valuations; what matters is how the business does long term, not the country.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He has spent time in South Korea, China, India and increasingly Turkey, with only a few Latin American investments; crazy leadership and policies in Latin America can mask really good companies.

ideas.idea: In Turkey 95-97% of stocks are uninvestible due to inflation, so a Turkish ETF is unhelpful; filter for companies with revenue in euros or dollars and Lira costs, which cuts 200 listed companies to about 10.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Example: a listed juice company with 98% of revenue exported to Europe, where Turkey has duty-free access, does really well under heavy inflation because Lira costs fall while euro revenue is stable.

ideas.idea: He will not invest in crypto because he does not understand it and does not need an opinion on everything; a productive life with plenty of returns is possible with no crypto.
ideas.detail: Crypto is like one of the 96 people at the cocktail party you do not need to figure out; he does not even understand blockchain well.

ideas.idea: Given a choice among Guy Spier, Buffett, Munger, Li Lu and Cathie Wood to manage his money, he would choose Li Lu.
ideas.detail: He joked it was very close between Li Lu and Cathie Wood. He also notes the baton is not being passed to him; Buffett and Munger have many great students and their writings remain forever.
